title: Rules of the Internet
note: There has never been one stable canonical 100-rule list. This archive preserves the familiar numbering and major recurring ideas while paraphrasing variants and adding historical context rather than presenting the rules as real laws.

rules.text: Do not talk about /b/.
Do not talk about /b/ again.
Anonymous is a collective identity, not a single person.
Anonymous is legion, in the language of the old meme.
The old Anonymous myth says it neither forgives nor forgets.
Anonymous can be chaotic, senseless, and uncaring.
Anonymous can still deliver when nobody expects it.
There are no real rules about posting, until a community enforces some.
There are no real rules about moderation either, but bans still happen.
Rival-site arguments are rarely worth your time.
Carefully prepared arguments can simply be ignored online.
Anything you post can be quoted or used against you later.
Anything you post can be remixed into something else.
Do not argue endlessly with trolls because attention is often the reward.
The harder you force a meme, the more likely it is to fail.
A spectacular failure can become a success as a meme.
Every online win eventually gets replaced by the next thing.
Anything that can be labeled can become a target of dislike.
The more attention a hated thing receives, the stronger its visibility can become.
Internet culture often refuses to take itself completely seriously.
Original content stops feeling original as soon as it is copied.
Copypasta exists to reproduce text until authorship becomes blurry.
Copypasta can itself become a new form of originality.
Reposting is one of the internet's oldest forms of distribution.
Every post can become someone else's context-free screenshot.
Every topic has someone willing to argue about it.
More users usually means more contradictory opinions.
Old imageboard folklore claimed there were no girls on the internet; this was a joke, not reality.
On the old anonymous web, identity claims were often treated skeptically.
Pictures and evidence became a running joke whenever someone made an extraordinary identity claim.
Attractive people are online too; the old rules were intentionally absurd about this.
The internet can turn ordinary people into temporary celebrities.
Lurking before posting is classic community advice.
If it exists, adult fan content of it probably exists somewhere. This is the famous Rule 34 meme.
If Rule 34 content does not exist yet, internet folklore jokes that it eventually will.
Anonymous folklore says grudges can last much longer online than expected.
Old rules about gender on the internet were jokes from anonymous-board culture, not factual statements.
Cats are always acceptable internet content.
One cat post tends to lead to another.
Cat memes multiply faster than anyone expects.
Almost anything can become somebody's niche interest or fetish.
Cake is often a joke, reference, reward, or lie depending on the fandom.
A suspiciously perfect offer may be a trap.
Every community eventually complains that the community is worse today.
Crude jokes spread quickly in anonymous spaces.
A favorite discontinued thing will be requested forever.
Self-deprecating jokes are a permanent part of internet culture.
When nobody knows what comes next, somebody will post question marks.
After the confusion, someone will claim profit.
Do not divide by zero in ordinary arithmetic.
The internet contains more information than any one user can finish reading.
Every fact online should be checked against better evidence when it matters.
A screenshot is evidence of a screen, not automatically evidence that the claim is true.
A viral claim can spread faster than its correction.
Someone has probably asked your question before.
Search before repeating a common question when an archive exists.
Every fandom develops its own vocabulary.
Every large fandom eventually develops internal drama.
Every platform produces its own style of humor.
Every platform eventually complains that another platform ruined the internet.
Nothing posted publicly should be assumed to remain unseen.
Deleted posts may survive in screenshots, caches, mirrors, or archives.
For many fictional characters, the internet creates gender-swapped interpretations. This is commonly called Rule 63.
For every popular character, someone will create an alternate-universe version.
If a format can be remixed, somebody will remix it.
If a song is popular, somebody will make a cover, remix, mashup, or parody.
If an image is recognizable, somebody will turn it into a reaction image.
If a phrase is repeatable, somebody will turn it into copypasta.
Numbers themselves can become memes when a community repeats them enough.
Someone will misunderstand an obvious joke.
Someone will take an obvious joke seriously.
Someone will respond to a serious post with a joke.
Extraordinary claims attract both believers and skeptics.
If a mystery remains unsolved, the internet will invent theories about it.
Every theory eventually gets a counter-theory.
If a file can be copied, copies will appear in unexpected places.
If a website disappears, someone may have archived part of it.
Broken links are part of web archaeology.
Old websites eventually become historical artifacts.
A typo can become the entire focus of a discussion.
A bad translation can become a famous quote.
A bug can become a feature if enough people enjoy it.
An obscure reference can become mainstream without warning.
The internet is serious business only when somebody insists that it is.
If it exists, somebody has probably made fan art of it.
If it exists, somebody has probably made a pony version of it.
If it exists, somebody has probably made a furry interpretation of it.
If software can be modified, somebody will try to mod it.
If hardware has a screen, somebody will try to run something unexpected on it.
If a device computes, somebody will benchmark it.
If an idea becomes popular, clones and variations appear quickly.
For every strong opinion, an equally strong opposing opinion can usually be found.
If it has a processor or display, somebody will try to run DOOM on it. This is a long-running hacker meme.
Any public identity can be impersonated, so verify important claims independently.
Somebody will be offended by almost any sufficiently widespread post.
Somebody will dislike any sufficiently popular thing.
For every joke, someone will miss the joke entirely.
If a display or medium can reproduce frames, somebody will try to play Bad Apple!! on it.
Memes that look permanent can vanish, while forgotten memes can return years later.
There is no final rulebook for the internet; every list is itself part of internet folklore.
